prompt: Use case: art-direction paintover for a skate park in a stylized open-world game. Image 1 is an in-game screenshot. Keep its camera, horizon and field of view, and keep every ramp, run, bowl and the terrain exactly where and how they are: do not move, reshape or remove any riding surface. Image 2 is the game's art direction for this park: keep its soft, flat, painterly island style, warm light and palette. The ramps float in the air with nothing under them. Paint the ramps as warm wooden skate ramps (ramp boards on top, plywood sides) and add supports that look designed and beautiful, not ugly: heavy timber trestle bents with diagonal cross bracing and visible joints, spaced rhythmically under every ramp and run, standing on squat dark volcanic-stone footings on the crater floor, tapering toward the top, and the tallest towers braced like old wooden roller-coaster trestles. Supports never cross the riding surface or the path of a jump through the air. Keep the crater floor natural volcanic rock and snow, not sand.

Use case: art-direction design for the support structures of a skate park in a stylized open-world game. Image 1 is an in-game screenshot: giant wooden skate ramps and a mega gap high on a volcano's crater rim, floating with nothing under them. Keep its camera, horizon, field of view, terrain and every ramp exactly where and how they are: do not move, reshape or remove any riding surface. Image 2 is the approved art direction: keep its soft painterly style, warm light, dark blue-grey columnar basalt, snow patches, yellow-green moss and autumn shrubs, and paint the ramps as warm wooden ramps with thin steel coping. The supports must look designed, calm and monumental, never like a forest of thin sticks: FEW large solid forms, each clearly readable, rising from the ground to meet the underside of the ramps. Design: a few monolithic basalt piers, widely spaced (about one every 40 to 50 metres), each a single massive solid pier as wide as the ramp, gently tapering upward and flaring into a broad capital that cradles the ramp's underside, its surface faceted with subtle vertical basalt column joints, its foot merging into a skirt of boulders and talus. No thin posts, no scaffolding.

Use case: art-direction design for the support structures of one skate line in a stylized open-world game. Image 1 is a plain 3D layout render from the park editor: flat-shaded ramps over a volcano's crater, untextured, with coloured route markings and red flight arcs that are not part of the art. Paint it as the finished in-game scene. Keep its camera, horizon and field of view, and keep every ramp, wall, bowl and the terrain exactly where and how they are: do not move, reshape or remove any riding surface. Image 2 is the approved art direction: keep its soft painterly style, warm light, dark blue-grey volcanic rock, yellow-green moss, a little snow on the ground only, and paint every riding surface as warm wooden skate ramp with thin steel coping (never snow on a ramp). The line: a rider drops from a Japanese start tower into the void onto an enormous wide curved catch wall, kicks off a towering near-vertical wall, lands on a tall reverse catch ramp, rides a giant U-turn bowl cut into the crater wall, then launches a huge kicker into a 150 m air onto a tall landing ramp that runs out on the crater floor. Today these ramps stand on plain dark blocks; replace every dark block with designed supports that look built and weathered, with few large readable forms, chamfered and layered, never thin sticks or plain boxes. Leave the air under every jump open. Design: a Japanese kakezukuri hillside-temple frame like the stage of Kiyomizu-dera: a deep orderly grid of massive weathered hinoki pillars braced by horizontal nuki tie-beams, stone footings and plinths at every post, the frames stepping down the slope; the tall catch wall and the reverse catch carried by these great timber stages, the U-turn bowl wrapped in a timber gallery, the landing ramp on a long stepped timber trestle.

Use case: art-direction design for the top of a skate start tower in a stylized open-world game. Image 1 is a plain 3D render: a square timber start deck about 22 by 16 m high on a Kiyomizu-style timber frame over a volcano crater, flat-shaded and untextured, with a small placeholder pavilion roof on it. Paint it as the finished in-game scene. Keep its camera, horizon and field of view, and keep the deck, the long plank roll-in leaving it, the huge curved wooden wall beside it and the timber frame below exactly where and how they are. Image 2 is the approved art direction: copy its look exactly: soft painterly style, warm light, warm wooden skate ramps with thin steel coping, massive weathered hinoki pillars with nuki tie-beams and stone footings, red-lacquer accents, dark volcanic rock with moss, a little snow on the ground only, never on a ramp. HARD RULE: the deck is where riders start: they run and roll across its whole surface and off its edges onto both ramps, so nothing may stand on the deck surface or in front of either ramp's start. Posts may only rise from the timber frame below, outside the deck's edges, or stand at the deck's outer corners on the railing line; anything overhead stays at least 6 m above the deck so it frames the riders, never blocks them. Remove the placeholder pavilion. Design: one great vermilion torii that frames the whole deck: its two massive round pillars rise from the timber frame below, just outside the deck's two side edges, on black stone footings, and its double lintel (kasagi and nuki) spans high over the deck with a gold plaque, so every rider starts by passing under the gate. Thick shimenawa rope with white paper shide hangs from the lintel well above head height.

Use case: art-direction concept for the boost walls of a skate park in a stylized open-world game. Image 1 is an in-game screenshot of the park's wooden flow bowl: a big bowl with curving transition walls, rounded U-turn bowl ends and the runs joining them, raised on supports over a volcanic crater floor. Paint it as the finished scene. Keep its camera, horizon and field of view, and keep every ramp, bowl wall, run, deck and the terrain exactly where and how they are: do not move, reshape, add or remove any riding surface. Image 2 is the approved art direction: copy its look exactly: soft painterly style, warm light, warm wooden skate ramps with thin steel coping, massive weathered hinoki timber frames with nuki tie-beams on stone footings under the ramps, dark volcanic rock with moss and autumn shrubs, snow only on the ground outside the park. Image 3 shows the park's graphic language: bold, flat, hand-painted 1970s pool graphics (bands and a sun) painted straight onto a skate bowl. The curved transition walls of the big bowl and of the rounded U-turn bowl ends are BOOST WALLS: pumping and powersliding on them gives speed, so they must be instantly recognizable from anywhere in the park and clearly unlike the plain wooden ramps. The long straight run along the right foreground is a normal run: keep it plain warm wood with steel coping, so the boost walls stand out against it. Every ridable surface stays a clean, smooth, skateable surface: no snow, rocks, props or clutter on any ramp, floor or deck, and all paint is flat and flush with the surface. Boost-wall treatment: painted chevron bands. Bold, evenly spaced hot-magenta chevrons (wide V-shaped stripes with a thin white outline) are painted on every boost transition, each chevron pointing straight up the wall toward the coping like a speed arrow, stacked from the flat bottom to the lip and repeating all the way round the bowl and the U-turns. Hot magenta appears nowhere else in the park. Warm wood shows between the chevrons; the flat bottom stays natural wood.

In the flat bottom at the centre of each boost bowl and U-turn sits a painted sun disc in sun-yellow, and broad rays alternating hot magenta and sun yellow radiate from it across the floor and run straight up every transition wall to the coping, widening as they climb, so from above the whole bowl reads as one huge sun and from inside every wall is rays shooting upward. The coping is painted bright gold. Hot magenta appears nowhere else in the park.
